senses.gloss: Making secret plans to get what you want, usually by tricking people.
examples: The show is full of *scheming* lawyers and crooked cops.
His *scheming* brother had already sold half the land.
She is far *more scheming* than she lets on.

contrast: The loose sense 'contradictory' offends many people, since it borrows a real illness as a metaphor. In writing, prefer *contradictory* or *inconsistent*.

senses.gloss: Having or relating to schizophrenia, a serious mental illness.
examples: He was treated at the clinic for *schizophrenic* episodes.
The book explains what *schizophrenic* symptoms actually look like.
Her brother is *schizophrenic* and has been stable for years.

senses.gloss: Pulling in two opposite directions at once.
examples: The company's *schizophrenic* marketing sells luxury and thrift in the same ad.
Policy on the region has been *schizophrenic* for a decade.

senses.gloss: So sentimental that it feels fake or embarrassing.
examples: The ending is *schmaltzy*, but I cried anyway.
He sang a *schmaltzy* ballad in a rented tuxedo.
Their second album is even *schmaltzier* than the first.

senses.gloss: Having to do with schools, studying and grades.
examples: Players have to keep up their *scholastic* standing to stay on the team.
She won a *scholastic* award for her work in chemistry.
The league covers *scholastic* sports across three states.

senses.gloss: Affecting every part of a school.
examples: The principal called a *schoolwide* assembly for Friday morning.
They ran a *schoolwide* survey about the new lunch menu.
The phone ban is *schoolwide*, not just in the math wing.

senses.gloss: Having to do with science.
examples: The journal publishes *scientific* research on sleep.
There is no *scientific* evidence for any of this.
She left teaching for a *scientific* career at a lab in Boston.

senses.gloss: Careful and organized, based on testing rather than guessing.
examples: He takes a *scientific* approach to picking a fantasy roster.
Tasting ten brands in one night is not exactly *scientific*.
Their hiring is *more scientific* than it used to be.

contrast: Often used sarcastically about something boring: *a scintillating lecture on tax forms*.

senses.gloss: Brilliantly lively and interesting.
examples: She is a *scintillating* speaker who never uses notes.
The conversation was hardly *scintillating*.
His *scintillating* second half won the game.

senses.gloss: Burned on the surface, or dried out and browned by heat.
examples: Nothing was left but *scorched* fields and black smoke.
The shirt had a *scorched* mark where the iron sat too long.
By August the lawn was completely *scorched*.

senses.gloss: Extremely hot.
examples: We walked four blocks in the *scorching* afternoon sun.
It was *scorching* by ten in the morning.
They played the whole game in *scorching* heat.

senses.gloss: Fiercely critical.
examples: The paper ran a *scorching* review of the restaurant.
She sent a *scorching* email to the whole department.

senses.gloss: With no points scored, in a game or a part of a game.
examples: The match ended in a *scoreless* tie.
Both teams were *scoreless* through three quarters.
The pitcher threw five *scoreless* innings.

senses.gloss: Showing that you think someone or something deserves no respect.
examples: She gave him a *scornful* look and walked out.
He is openly *scornful* of anyone who studies for the test.
The critics were *more scornful* of the sequel than of the original.

contrast: Ends in *-ly* but is an adjective, not an adverb.

senses.gloss: Growing in thin, uneven, untidy patches.
examples: He showed up with a *scraggly* beard and no jacket.
A few *scraggly* pines grew along the ridge.
The lawn looked *scragglier* every week we skipped it.

senses.gloss: Cooked by beating the eggs together and stirring them in a pan.
examples: I had *scrambled* eggs and toast for breakfast.
She likes her eggs *scrambled*, not fried.
The diner serves *scrambled* eggs all day.

senses.gloss: Mixed up out of order, or coded so that it cannot be read or heard.
examples: The letters came through *scrambled* and nobody could read them.
The channel is *scrambled* unless you pay for it.

contrast: In American English this is praise — small but tough. British *scrappy* means 'messy, thrown together', which is an insult.

senses.gloss: Fighting hard and never giving up, especially against bigger opponents.
examples: They are a *scrappy* team that wins games they should lose.
He was a *scrappy* kid who never backed down.
The *scrappier* of the two candidates took the debate.

senses.gloss: Rough enough against the skin to itch.
examples: The blanket is warm but *scratchy*.
She hated the *scratchy* tag inside the collar.
This sweater is *scratchier* than the wool one.

senses.gloss: Rough and uneven in sound.
examples: His voice was *scratchy* after two nights of shouting.
The recording is *scratchy*, but you can hear the words.

contrast: *Scrawny* is unkind; *slim* and *slender* are compliments.

senses.gloss: Unpleasantly thin and weak-looking.
examples: He was a *scrawny* teenager who ate constantly.
A *scrawny* cat was waiting on the porch.
The chicken they served was even *scrawnier* than the last one.

contrast: Also a noun: *a screwball* is an oddball, and in baseball a pitch that breaks the wrong way.

senses.gloss: Crazy in a funny, unpredictable way, used above all of comedy.
examples: We watched a *screwball* comedy from the 1930s.
The plot takes a *screwball* turn in the second act.
She has a *screwball* sense of humor that wins people over.

senses.gloss: Written out in advance instead of said or done spontaneously.
examples: Network television still runs mostly *scripted* dramas.
His apology sounded *scripted*.
The town hall felt *more scripted* than the debate did.

senses.gloss: Untidy and worn-looking.
examples: A *scruffy* dog followed us the whole way home.
He turned up *scruffy* and an hour late.
The neighborhood looks *scruffier* than it did ten years ago.

contrast: Warm and a little old-fashioned; *delicious* is the neutral word.

senses.gloss: Extremely good to eat.
examples: Her grandmother makes a *scrumptious* peach pie.
Everything on the table looked *scrumptious*.
The bread was warm and absolutely *scrumptious*.

senses.gloss: Careful to do everything correctly and honestly, down to small details.
examples: She is *scrupulous* about paying people on time.
The report was based on *scrupulous* record keeping.
He is *more scrupulous* than anyone else in that office.

senses.gloss: Shaped by carving or modeling.
examples: A *sculpted* stone lion sits at each end of the bridge.
The doors are covered in *sculpted* panels.

senses.gloss: Firm and clearly shaped, as if carved, said of a body or a face.
examples: He has the *sculpted* arms of someone who lives at the gym.
Her cheekbones look *sculpted*.

senses.gloss: Insulting and almost certainly untrue, said or written to damage someone.
examples: The campaign spread *scurrilous* rumors about his family.
She sued the site over a *scurrilous* article.
The attacks grew *more scurrilous* as the vote got closer.

senses.gloss: Traveling by sea, or living by work at sea.
examples: The Portuguese were a great *seafaring* nation.
He came from a long line of *seafaring* men.
The museum tells the story of the town's *seafaring* past.

senses.gloss: Closed so tightly that nothing can get in or out.
examples: Bring the form back in a *sealed* envelope.
The meat comes in a *sealed* plastic tray.
Every window in the building is *sealed* shut.

senses.gloss: Closed by a court or an official so that the public cannot see it.
examples: His juvenile record is *sealed*.
The indictment stayed *sealed* until the arrest.

senses.gloss: Moving from one part to the next with no gap, break or trouble.
examples: The handoff between the two crews was *seamless*.
They promise a *seamless* transfer of your old files.
The new checkout is *more seamless* than the old one.

senses.gloss: Made in one piece, with no sewn or welded joins.
examples: The pipe is drawn as a single *seamless* tube.
She wore a *seamless* knit dress.

senses.gloss: Trying hard to find out the truth about someone or something.
examples: She gave him a long, *searching* look.
The reporter asked a few *searching* questions about the money.
The book is a *searching* account of his own failures.

senses.gloss: Browned fast over high heat on the outside.
examples: The special is *seared* tuna with a sesame crust.
Serve the steak *seared* on both sides but still pink inside.
A *seared* scallop should be dark gold, not gray.

senses.gloss: Burning hot, or painful like a burn.
examples: A *searing* pain shot down his leg.
They crossed the desert in *searing* heat.
The wind off the pavement was *searing*.

senses.gloss: Sharply critical or emotionally intense.
examples: The film is a *searing* portrait of life on the border.
She wrote a *searing* letter to the board.

senses.gloss: Sick to your stomach because of the movement of a boat.
examples: Half the passengers were *seasick* within an hour.
Take a pill before you board if you get *seasick*.
He looked *seasick* the whole way across.

contrast: *Seasonal* means 'tied to a season'; *seasoned* means 'experienced' or 'flavored'.

senses.gloss: Happening in, or changing with, a particular time of year.
examples: The store hires *seasonal* workers every November.
*Seasonal* allergies hit him hard in the spring.
Demand for the product is highly *seasonal*.

position: both — the 'experienced' sense goes before a noun

senses.gloss: Having a lot of experience at something.
examples: She is a *seasoned* negotiator who has seen every trick.
Even *seasoned* climbers turn back in that weather.

senses.gloss: Given flavor with salt, pepper or herbs.
examples: The soup was perfectly *seasoned*.
Use lightly *seasoned* ground beef for the filling.

senses.gloss: Sitting down, or done while sitting.
examples: Please remain *seated* until the plane reaches the gate.
The class ends with a *seated* stretch.
She was already *seated* when I got there.

senses.gloss: In good enough condition to sail safely.
examples: The inspector declared the boat *seaworthy*.
It took two years to make the old schooner *seaworthy* again.
Nobody would call that raft a *seaworthy* vessel.

senses.gloss: Quiet and private, far from other people.
examples: They rented a *secluded* cabin in the mountains.
There is a *secluded* beach on the far side of the island.
The back patio is *more secluded* than the front porch.

contrast: Also a noun (*a second* of time) and a verb (*to second a motion*). In *I finished second* it is the adverb.

senses.gloss: Coming right after the first.
examples: Her office is the *second* door on the left.
He struck out in the *second* inning.
This is the *second* time this week.

senses.gloss: One more of the same kind.
examples: Give him a *second* chance.
Would you like a *second* helping?

contrast: Also a noun in *settle for second best*, written without the hyphen.

senses.gloss: Not quite as good as the best one.
examples: He wore his *second-best* suit to the interview.
Their offer was the *second-best* on the table.
Taking the bus is *second-best*, but it works.

senses.gloss: Treated as less important, with fewer rights than other people.
examples: They were treated like *second-class* citizens in their own country.
No student should get a *second-class* education because of a zip code.

senses.gloss: Of the cheaper grade of travel or mail.
examples: He rode in a *second-class* car all the way to Chicago.
The magazine went out at *second-class* postage rates.

senses.gloss: Clearly not very good.
examples: It was a *second-rate* hotel with a good view.
He spent years writing *second-rate* thrillers.
The food is fine; the service is *second-rate*.

form: compound — *second* + *string*, from the lineup of players

senses.gloss: Not in the starting lineup, or not in the top group.
examples: The *second-string* quarterback finished the game.
They sent a *second-string* delegation to the talks.
He spent two seasons as a *second-string* catcher.

senses.gloss: In the second year of a course, a job or a career.
examples: She is a *second-year* law student.
The team is built around a *second-year* point guard.
*Second-year* residents take the night shifts.

senses.gloss: Less important than something else.
examples: Cost is *secondary* to safety here.
The plot is *secondary*; you watch it for the acting.
Those are *secondary* concerns we can handle later.

senses.gloss: Of the school years between elementary school and college.
examples: He teaches at the *secondary* level.
Fewer than half of them finished *secondary* school.

contrast: Also a noun: *keep a secret*. The person who holds things back is *secretive*, not *secret*.

senses.gloss: Known to only a few people and deliberately kept from everyone else.
examples: They held a *secret* meeting in the back office.
He had a *secret* second phone.
The vote is *secret*, so nobody sees your ballot.

senses.gloss: Hidden so that other people cannot find it.
examples: There is a *secret* door behind the bookcase.
She kept the letters in a *secret* compartment.

senses.gloss: Having to do with the work of a secretary.
examples: She took a *secretarial* course after high school.
The job is mostly *secretarial* duties and scheduling.
He was hired for *secretarial* work at a law firm.

contrast: *Secretive* describes a person or an organization that hides things; *secret* describes the thing that is hidden.

senses.gloss: Keeping your plans and feelings to yourself.
examples: He was *secretive* about where the money came from.
The company is famously *secretive* about new products.
She got *more secretive* as the divorce dragged on.

senses.gloss: Coming from the split between religious or political groups, often violently.
examples: *Sectarian* violence broke out again in the capital.
The country is still divided along *sectarian* lines.
He warned that the debate was becoming *more sectarian* than practical.

senses.gloss: Not connected with religion or the church.
examples: Public schools here are *secular* by law.
He writes *secular* music for a church choir to sing.
The country has grown *more secular* over two generations.

senses.gloss: Safe from attack, theft or danger.
examples: Keep the files on a *secure* server.
The building is *more secure* than it looks.
She finally found a *secure* job with benefits.

senses.gloss: Firmly fixed so that it will not move or come loose.
examples: Make sure the ladder is *secure* before you climb.
Check that the straps are *secure*.

senses.gloss: Feeling confident and not worried.
examples: Kids need to feel *secure* at home.
He is *secure* in the knowledge that his family backs him.

contrast: Also a verb: *to sedate a patient* is to give them a calming drug. The adjective does not mean 'drugged'.

senses.gloss: Calm, slow and rather formal.
examples: They went for a *sedate* walk around the pond.
The party was a *sedate* affair with classical music.
Life on the island is *more sedate* than in the city.

contrast: Much more common as a noun: *the doctor gave her a sedative*.

senses.gloss: Having the effect of calming a person down or making them sleepy.
examples: The drug has a mild *sedative* effect.
*Sedative* properties make it useful before surgery.
They warned him about the *sedative* side effects.

senses.gloss: Involving a lot of sitting and very little exercise.
examples: Twelve hours at a desk makes for a *sedentary* job.
A *sedentary* lifestyle raises your risk of heart disease.
He has gotten *more sedentary* since he started working from home.

senses.gloss: Formed from layers of sand, mud or shells pressed together over time.
examples: Sandstone and limestone are *sedimentary* rocks.
The canyon walls show bands of *sedimentary* layers.
Oil is usually found in *sedimentary* basins.

senses.gloss: Encouraging people to rebel against the government.
examples: He was arrested for printing *seditious* pamphlets.
The speech was condemned as *seditious*.
The later letters are *more seditious* than anything he published.

senses.gloss: Sexually attractive in a deliberate way.
examples: She sang the whole song in a low, *seductive* voice.
He gave her a *seductive* smile across the room.

senses.gloss: Tempting, because it makes a bad idea look good.
examples: There is something *seductive* about a simple answer.
The argument is *more seductive* than it is sound.

contrast: Used of clothing and thin fabric; for glass and water the word is *clear* or *transparent*.

senses.gloss: Thin enough that you can see what is behind or under it.
examples: She wore a *see-through* blouse over a tank top.
The shower curtain is almost *see-through*.
They packed everything in *see-through* bags for security.

senses.gloss: Ranked among the top players or teams in a tournament.
examples: The top-*seeded* team lost in the first round.
She is *seeded* third at the Open this year.

senses.gloss: Planted with seed.
examples: Keep off the newly *seeded* lawn.
A freshly *seeded* field needs water twice a day.

senses.gloss: Grown without seeds or pits.
examples: Get the *seedless* grapes, not the ones with pits.
*Seedless* watermelon is easier to feed to kids.
The green ones are *seedless*.

senses.gloss: Run-down and slightly dishonest or unsafe.
examples: They stayed in a *seedy* motel off the highway.
The bar has a *seedy* reputation.
The block gets *seedier* the closer you get to the station.

contrast: Never after a verb — you cannot say *the calm was seeming*. The adverb *seemingly* is far more common.

senses.gloss: Appearing to be true, though it may not be.
examples: Her *seeming* calm hid a lot of panic.
Despite his *seeming* indifference, he read every word.
The *seeming* contradiction disappears once you read the footnote.

senses.gloss: Extremely angry but holding it in.
examples: He sat through the whole meeting *seething*.
She was *seething* with resentment by the end of the trip.

senses.gloss: Full of crowded, restless movement.
examples: The market was a *seething* mass of people.
The river below was *seething* and brown.

senses.gloss: Kept apart by race, sex or class, usually unfairly.
examples: His parents grew up in a *segregated* school system.
Housing in the city is still deeply *segregated*.
Some districts are *more segregated* now than they were in 1970.

senses.gloss: Having to do with earthquakes.
examples: The bridge was built to the latest *seismic* standards.
*Seismic* activity picked up under the volcano.

senses.gloss: Enormous and sudden, said of change.
examples: The ruling was a *seismic* shift in the law.
Streaming had a *seismic* effect on the music business.

contrast: Also a common verb (*select a file*). As an adjective it goes only before a noun.

senses.gloss: Chosen as the best, and open to only a few.
examples: Only a *select* few were invited to the dinner.
The wine list includes some *select* California reds.
He plays on a *select* travel team.

contrast: *Selected* means someone picked them out; *select* means they are the best. *Selected poems* is a sample, *a select group* is an elite.

senses.gloss: Picked out from a larger group.
examples: The volume prints his *selected* essays from twenty years.
The sale runs on *selected* items only.
*Selected* students get to sit in on the seminar.

senses.gloss: Choosing carefully, and taking only a few.
examples: She is very *selective* about who she works with.
The college is *more selective* than it was a decade ago.

senses.gloss: Affecting or including some things but not others.
examples: He has a *selective* memory about that night.
The policy amounts to *selective* enforcement.

senses.gloss: So interested in your own life that you barely notice other people.
examples: He is too *self-absorbed* to ask how anyone else is doing.
The narrator is a *self-absorbed* twenty-year-old.
She gets *more self-absorbed* every time she is in a play.

senses.gloss: Carrying your own name and address, so that it can be mailed back to you.
examples: Include a *self-addressed* stamped envelope with your entry.
They mailed the results back in the *self-addressed* envelope.
The form asks for a *self-addressed* postcard.

senses.gloss: Working to make yourself look more important than you are.
examples: The memoir is a long, *self-aggrandizing* account of one lucky deal.
He made a *self-aggrandizing* speech about his own generosity.
Each retelling gets *more self-aggrandizing*.

senses.gloss: Having taken a job or a role without anyone asking you to.
examples: He is the *self-appointed* guardian of the block's parking spots.
A *self-appointed* committee rewrote the bylaws.
She acts as the *self-appointed* spokesperson for the neighborhood.

contrast: *Self-assured* is a compliment; *self-satisfied* and *smug* are not.

senses.gloss: Calmly confident in your own abilities.
examples: She walked into the room *self-assured* and unhurried.
He gave a *self-assured* answer to a hostile question.
He is *more self-assured* on stage than he is in conversation.

senses.gloss: Able to see your own faults and how you come across to others.
examples: For a nineteen-year-old he is remarkably *self-aware*.
The show is *self-aware* about how silly its own premise is.
She got *more self-aware* after a year of therapy.

contrast: American *self-centered*; British writing spells it *self-centred*.

senses.gloss: Thinking only about yourself and what you want.
examples: He is too *self-centered* to notice that she was upset.
It was a *self-centered* thing to say at a funeral.
Teenagers can be *more self-centered* than they mean to be.

senses.gloss: Admitted by the person themselves, usually about a fault or a habit.
examples: He is a *self-confessed* workaholic.
The book was written by a *self-confessed* amateur.
She is a *self-confessed* fan of bad reality TV.

contrast: A false friend: it does not mean 'сознательный'. It means uncomfortable about how you look or sound.

senses.gloss: Uncomfortably aware of how other people are seeing you.
examples: She is *self-conscious* about her accent.
He gave a *self-conscious* laugh and looked at the floor.
I felt *more self-conscious* in that room than anywhere else.

senses.gloss: Deliberately aware of its own style, said of art and writing.
examples: The film is full of *self-conscious* references to old westerns.
The prose is *self-conscious* in a way that gets tiring.

senses.gloss: Complete in itself, with everything it needs inside it.
examples: Each episode is a *self-contained* story.
The guest house is *self-contained*, with its own kitchen.

senses.gloss: Keeping to yourself and not needing other people's company.
examples: He is a quiet, *self-contained* man who reads all evening.
She seemed perfectly *self-contained* at the party.

senses.gloss: Containing two statements that cannot both be true.
examples: His testimony was *self-contradictory* from the first page.
The rule is *self-contradictory*: it bans what the next line requires.
That is a *self-contradictory* way to describe a free market.

senses.gloss: Working against the very thing you are trying to achieve.
examples: Cutting the training budget to save money is *self-defeating*.
He is stuck in a *self-defeating* cycle of quitting and starting over.
Their strategy turned out to be *more self-defeating* than risky.

contrast: Usually charming rather than sad: it is making fun of yourself before anyone else can.

senses.gloss: Making light of your own abilities or achievements.
examples: His speech was funny and *self-deprecating*.
She made a *self-deprecating* joke about her cooking.
He is *more self-deprecating* in interviews than he is in person.

senses.gloss: Harming yourself by the way you behave.
examples: Drinking before every shift was *self-destructive* and he knew it.
The band fell apart in a *self-destructive* spiral.
His choices got *more self-destructive* after the injury.

senses.gloss: Organized and driven by the person doing it, without a teacher or a boss.
examples: The course is *self-directed*, with deadlines you set yourself.
He opened a *self-directed* retirement account.
Graduate work is *more self-directed* than college.

senses.gloss: Able to make yourself do what needs doing without being pushed.
examples: You have to be *self-disciplined* to work from home.
She is the *most self-disciplined* runner on the team.
He is a quiet, *self-disciplined* kid.

senses.gloss: Having learned by reading and studying alone rather than at a school.
examples: He was a *self-educated* engineer who never finished high school.
She is largely *self-educated* in music theory.
The library was full of *self-educated* readers.

senses.gloss: Not wanting attention or credit for what you have done.
examples: He is so *self-effacing* that nobody knew he had funded the whole thing.
She gave a short, *self-effacing* answer and changed the subject.
The coach is *more self-effacing* than most people in the job.

senses.gloss: Working for yourself rather than for a company.
examples: She has been *self-employed* since 2015.
*Self-employed* people pay their taxes quarterly.
He left the firm to become a *self-employed* consultant.

senses.gloss: Obviously true without needing any proof.
examples: We hold these truths to be *self-evident*.
It is *self-evident* that the two numbers cannot both be right.
The answer is not as *self-evident* as he thinks.

ru: не требующий пояснений, понятный сам по себе

senses.gloss: Clear on its own, with no explanation needed.
examples: The instructions are *self-explanatory*.
Most of the buttons are *self-explanatory* once you open the app.
The chart is *more self-explanatory* than the paragraph under it.

senses.gloss: Running its own affairs without being controlled from outside.
examples: The territory has been *self-governing* since 1979.
Each *self-governing* district sets its own school calendar.
The profession is largely *self-governing*.

senses.gloss: Acting as if you matter far more than you do.
examples: A *self-important* little man checked our badges twice.
The email was long and *self-important*.
He gets *more self-important* with every promotion.

senses.gloss: Chosen by yourself rather than forced on you by someone else.
examples: He missed his own *self-imposed* deadline by a month.
She spent a year in *self-imposed* exile in Maine.
The company works under a *self-imposed* limit on overtime.

senses.gloss: Brought on by your own actions.
examples: The whole crisis was *self-induced*.
He blamed his *self-induced* panic on too much coffee.
It was a *self-induced* injury from lifting too much too fast.

senses.gloss: Letting yourself have whatever you want, more than is good for you.
examples: A whole Saturday in bed felt gloriously *self-indulgent*.
He has a *self-indulgent* streak when it comes to gadgets.

senses.gloss: Too long or too pleased with itself, said of art and writing.
examples: The director's cut is *self-indulgent* at three and a half hours.
Critics called the album *more self-indulgent* than his last one.

contrast: A close synonym of *self-absorbed*; American writers use both.

senses.gloss: Wrapped up in your own problems and feelings.
examples: He was too *self-involved* that year to see what she was going through.
The characters are all young and *self-involved*.
Grief made her *more self-involved* than usual.

senses.gloss: Rich or successful through your own work, starting with nothing.
examples: He likes to call himself a *self-made* millionaire.
She is a *self-made* businesswoman from a mill town.
The magazine ran a list of *self-made* founders under thirty.

senses.gloss: Calm and in control of yourself under pressure.
examples: She stayed *self-possessed* through two hours of questions.
He is a *self-possessed* witness who never raises his voice.
The younger sister is *more self-possessed* than either parent.

contrast: Usually skeptical: the writer is signaling that only this person makes the claim.

senses.gloss: Called that by the person themselves, with nobody else agreeing.
examples: A *self-proclaimed* expert ran the whole workshop.
The *self-proclaimed* king of neighborhood barbecue lost the contest.
He is a *self-proclaimed* political outsider with thirty years in office.

senses.gloss: Carrying its own engine or motor instead of being pushed or pulled.
examples: The army bought a battery of *self-propelled* guns.
He mows the hill with a *self-propelled* mower.
A *self-propelled* barge came up the channel.

senses.gloss: Able to manage without help from other people.
examples: Living alone made him *self-reliant* fast.
She raised three *self-reliant* daughters.
The town is *more self-reliant* than it was before the mill closed.

contrast: Nine times out of ten it follows *no*: *no self-respecting cook would buy that*.

senses.gloss: Having proper pride in yourself and your standards.
examples: No *self-respecting* barbecue joint serves that sauce.
No *self-respecting* editor would let that headline through.
Any *self-respecting* fan knows the whole roster.

senses.gloss: Sure that you are more moral than everyone else, and showing it.
examples: He gave a *self-righteous* lecture about recycling.
The tone of the letter is *self-righteous* and a little cruel.
She gets *more self-righteous* every time the subject comes up.

senses.gloss: Giving up your own comfort or wishes for other people.
examples: Her mother was a *self-sacrificing* woman who worked two jobs.
It was a *self-sacrificing* decision that cost him the promotion.
Nurses on that ward are *more self-sacrificing* than anyone knows.
